etymology: From the Hebrew malluach, itself from melach, “salt” — the salt-plant or sea-purslane that grows in briny waste ground. The AV renders it mallows: a coarse, saltish herb, no man’s chosen dish, gathered by the destitute for want of bread.
biblical_def: Mallows is a famine-herb. The word stands but once in the AV, and it stands in a lament: “Who cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots for their meat” (Job 30:4). The salt-plant of the waste ground is not a garnish but a last resort, torn up by the roots where nothing better grows. Job draws the picture whole. These were men “for want and famine… solitary; fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste” (Job 30:3); men “driven forth from among men, (they cried after them as after a thief;)” (Job 30:5). Hunger is here what Scripture always makes it: a fruit of the curse upon the ground (Gen 3:17–19), and a rod in the LORD’s hand. Yet Job’s complaint is not that men are poor. His complaint is that the basest men, whose fathers he would have disdained to set with the dogs of his flock, now sit in judgment upon a righteous man — the fear of God overturned and the mocker enthroned. Jeremiah saw the same overturning from the other side: “They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills” (Lam 4:5). Scripture never romanticises want, and never despises the man who suffers it. The LORD who feeds the ravens (Psa 147:9) numbers such men; and the Son of God, who had not where to lay His head (Mat 8:20), took the outcast’s portion that He might bring outcasts home.
webster_summary: A coarse salt-herb of waste ground, gathered for food by the destitute; the plant of famine, not of the table.
webster_full: MALLOWS, a plant of the waste and salty ground, of little worth as food, eaten only in extremity.
From the Hebrew malluach, from melach, “salt” — the salt-plant or sea-purslane.
It names not a delicacy but the last shift of a starving man.
It occurs once in the Authorized Version, in Job’s lament (Job 30:4).
It is gathered with juniper roots by men driven out from among men.
scriptures: Job 30:4
Who cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots for their meat.
Job 30:3
For want and famine they were solitary; fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste.
Job 30:5
They were driven forth from among men, (they cried after them as after a thief;)
Lam 4:5
They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills.
corruption_summary: A word for the food of the destitute — and our age has learned to read want as a verdict on the sufferer’s faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the prosperity gospel, which turns Job’s mallows into evidence against the man who eats them. In that teaching — from Kenyon and Hagin down through the health-and-wealth pulpits of our own day — poverty is not affliction but diagnosis: the empty hand proves an empty confession, and the believer who is hungry has failed to name and claim. Job’s comforters said as much in older language, and the LORD answered them out of the whirlwind. Scripture knows poor saints and rich fools, and it knows a Lazarus full of sores carried into Abraham’s bosom while a purple-clothed man lifts up his eyes in torment (Luk 16:19–25). To read a man’s bank as his standing before God is to read the Bible backward, and it leaves the afflicted brother twice wounded — once by want, and once by the pulpit that blames him for it.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of daily bread. The LORD teaches His people to ask for it (Mat 6:11), which means He does not promise a storehouse but a day’s supply, and He does not despise the hand that must ask. Agur’s prayer is the balanced petition: neither poverty that tempts to steal nor riches that tempt to forget (Pro 30:8–9). And the church has a plain duty toward the man reduced to mallows — not a slogan but a loaf: “If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?” (Jas 2:15–16). Christ was made poor that we through His poverty might be rich (2Co 8:9); that is the only prosperity the gospel promises, and it is enough.
roots_summary: The word names a salt-herb of the waste ground, eaten only by the starving.
roots_lines: Mallows — Hebrew malluach, from melach, “salt.”
It denotes the salt-plant or sea-purslane of briny waste ground.
It is famine-food, cut up by the bushes where nothing better grows (Job 30:4).
It stands beside juniper roots in the diet of the destitute.
It occurs but once in the Authorized Version.
usage: Mallows is not a dish but a last resort — the herb of men who have no bread.
They cut up mallows by the bushes: hunger drives a man to the salt waste.
Job’s grief was not that men ate mallows, but that such men now mocked the righteous.

etymology: From the Latin juniperus. In the AV it renders the Hebrew rothem, the white broom of the desert — a tall, scanty shrub of the southern wilderness whose thin shade is the only shelter for miles and whose roots make the hottest and longest-burning coals.
biblical_def: The juniper of Scripture is the desert broom, and it is chiefly known by one man who slept under it. Elijah, fresh from Carmel and fleeing Jezebel’s oath, went a day’s journey into the wilderness, sat down under a juniper tree, and asked to die (1Ki 19:4). Here is a true prophet of the LORD, of like passions with us (Jas 5:17), sunk so low that death looks like mercy. Mark how the LORD deals with him. There is no rebuke first, and no indulgence either. There is sleep: “And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat” (1Ki 19:5). There is food: “a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head” (1Ki 19:6). There is a second touch and a reason — “the journey is too great for thee” (1Ki 19:7). Then, and only then, forty days to Horeb, the wind and earthquake and fire, the still small voice, a searching question twice asked, a fresh commission, and the word that seven thousand knees had never bowed to Baal. God restored His prophet by bread and sleep and then by His word, and He sent him back to work. The wood serves elsewhere as an emblem of judgment — the false tongue is answered with “sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper” (Psa 120:4) — and its roots are the meat of the destitute (Job 30:4).
webster_summary: The desert broom of the AV; a scanty shrub giving thin shade, whose roots yield the fiercest coals.
webster_full: JUNIPER, a shrub or low tree of the waste places; in Scripture the desert broom, Hebrew rothem.
From the Latin juniperus.
Its shade is thin, yet it is the only shelter in the southern wilderness.
Its roots burn hot and long, whence “coals of juniper” (Psa 120:4).
Elijah sat and slept beneath it when he requested to die (1Ki 19:4–5).
scriptures: And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat.
And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again.
And the angel of the LORD came again the second time, and touched him, and said, Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee.
Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper.
corruption_summary: The juniper text is now commonly preached as a case study, with the diagnosis kept and the LORD’s word at Horeb cut out.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the therapeutic reduction of 1 Kings 19. The chapter is handed over to the counselling clinic: Elijah is a study in exhaustion, the angel’s cake becomes a lesson in nutrition, the sleep becomes a lesson in rest, and the sermon ends there — before Horeb, before the still small voice, before the twice-repeated question that searched the prophet’s heart, before the commission that sent him back to anoint kings, and before the seven thousand that answered his self-pity with fact. What is left is a chapter about a tired man managing himself, when Scripture wrote a chapter about the living God restoring His servant. Bread and sleep are genuinely there, and God gave them; but He gave them as the first mercies of a longer dealing, not as the whole cure. Strip out the word of the LORD and the passage no longer preaches the LORD at all.

The opposite error must be named too: the affected piety that denies a saint can sink. Some pulpits treat Elijah’s request to die as simple unbelief to be scolded, and so they teach the afflicted brother to hide. Scripture is more honest and more tender than either party. It records the prophet’s words without excusing them and without shaming him for them; it names his despondency, and it shows God answering with an angel’s touch rather than a lecture. The Psalms speak the same way — “Why art thou cast down, O my soul?… hope thou in God” (Psa 42:11) — a real question honestly asked, and then the soul commanded back to its Rock. The pattern is: the LORD supplies the body, speaks to the soul, and restores the man to his work. Neither the clinic nor the scold can do that.
roots_summary: The word names the desert broom — thin shade above, fierce coals below.
roots_lines: Juniper — Latin juniperus; in the AV the Hebrew rothem, the desert broom.
It is a scanty shrub of the southern wilderness, its shade the only shelter for miles.
Elijah sat and slept under it and requested that he might die (1Ki 19:4–5).
Its roots yield coals of unusual heat and endurance (Psa 120:4).
Those roots were meat for the destitute in Job’s lament (Job 30:4).
usage: Under the juniper tree a true prophet asked to die — and God sent bread, not a rebuke.
The juniper gives thin shade; the angel’s cake and the cruse of water gave more.
Coals of juniper burn longest: so the Psalmist pictures the answer to a false tongue.

etymology: From the Greek sykomoraia, from sykon, “fig,” and moron, “mulberry” — the fig-mulberry of Egypt and the Judean lowland, a broad low-branching tree bearing a coarse, cheap fig. Not the modern plane or maple that now carries the name.
biblical_def: The sycomore is the poor man’s fig. Its fruit is plentiful and cheap, it grows thick in the vale, and its low limbs are easily climbed. Solomon’s wealth is measured by it: he “made cedars to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance” (1Ki 10:27) — the costly made as common as the commonest tree in Israel. Two men in Scripture stand out by it. The first is Amos, who answered Amaziah the court priest, “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit” (Amo 7:14). He had neither pedigree nor school; he had a call: “And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel” (Amo 7:15). The sovereign call, not the credential, makes a prophet. The second is Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans and rich, small of stature, who did the undignified thing and “ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him” (Luk 19:4). Christ stopped beneath it, called him by name, and lodged with him that day. The man sought the Saviour because the Saviour had first sought the man: “the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luk 19:10). One tree, two mercies — a herdman made a prophet, and a chief publican made a son of Abraham.
webster_summary: The fig-mulberry of Egypt and the Judean lowland; a common tree bearing coarse cheap figs, easily climbed.
webster_full: SYCOMORE, a tree of the fig kind, bearing a coarse fruit; common in Egypt and the low country of Judea.
From the Greek sykomoraia — sykon, “fig,” and moron, “mulberry.”
It is not the plane or maple which now bears the name in English use.
Its abundance measured Solomon’s wealth: cedars made as sycomores (1Ki 10:27).
Amos gathered its fruit; Zacchaeus climbed its branches (Amo 7:14; Luk 19:4).
scriptures: Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Amo 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
Luk 19:4
And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way.
For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
corruption_summary: The tree of the uncredentialed prophet, in an age that will hear no man who cannot first show a platform.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern credentialing of the ministry — not the sober training of men, which Scripture commends, but the substitution of platform for call. Amaziah’s objection to Amos was institutional: this is the king’s chapel, go prophesy in Judah and eat bread there. The prophet answered with his want of pedigree and the LORD’s appointment. Our age has its own Amaziahs, who weigh a man by his following, his conference invitations, his book contract, and his reach, and who cannot conceive that God still takes herdmen from the flock. The result is pulpits filled by the marketable and emptied of the sent. Scripture’s order is otherwise: “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15). The church is charged to try and to ordain men by the qualifications of 1Ti 3 and Tit 1 — character, aptness to teach, a household ruled well — and not one of those tests is a measure of audience.

The counter-corruption is equally live: the man who quotes Amos to excuse his own contempt for learning and for the church’s examination. Amos was untrained, but he was not unsent, and he was not unaccountable; his word was the LORD’s word, and it stood the test of Scripture and of fulfilment. The lawful order remains: God calls whom He will, the church tries and confirms that call, and the man labours under elders. Against both errors stands the sycomore of Luk 19. Zacchaeus had no qualification whatever — a chief publican, a collaborator, a rich thief — and grace found him in a tree. That is the doctrine both parties need: the call is sovereign, and so is the salvation.
roots_summary: The word names the fig-mulberry — a common tree, cheap fruit, low branches.
roots_lines: Sycomore — Greek sykomoraia, “fig-mulberry.”
It bears a coarse, plentiful fig, the food of ordinary men.
Its abundance in the vale measured Solomon’s wealth (1Ki 10:27).
Amos was “a gatherer of sycomore fruit” before the LORD took him (Amo 7:14).
Its low limbs let a short man climb to see Christ pass (Luk 19:4).
usage: A gatherer of sycomore fruit was made a prophet: the call is the LORD’s, not the school’s.
The sycomore was the commonest tree in the vale — and grace stopped under one.
Zacchaeus climbed a sycomore to see Christ; Christ had already come to seek Zacchaeus.

etymology: From the Hebrew almuggim, appearing by metathesis as algummim in Chronicles — a costly imported timber, most probably the red sandalwood of the East, close-grained, fragrant, and fit alike for building and for the making of instruments of music.
biblical_def: Almug is the finest timber named in Scripture, and it is named only in the building of the house of the LORD. Hiram’s navy fetched it from Ophir with gold and precious stones: “the navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones” (1Ki 10:11). What Solomon did with it is the point. “And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD, and for the king’s house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day” (1Ki 10:12). Note the order: the house of the LORD first, the king’s house second. The best of the best went to the sanctuary before it went to the palace, and what remained went to praise. The Chronicler records the same, calling the timber algum and the work terraces: “and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah” (2Ch 9:11). Here is the wealth of the nations sailing to Zion by the LORD’s ordering, exactly as Isaiah foretold — the glory of Lebanon brought “to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). And here is worship built and sung upon rarest wood, that the congregation might have pillars beneath it and harps before it. Yet the temple was a shadow; the substance is Christ, in whom “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9).
webster_summary: A rare and costly timber brought from Ophir, used for the pillars of the temple and for harps and psalteries.
webster_full: ALMUG, a precious wood of the East, brought by Solomon’s navy from Ophir; called algum in Chronicles.
From the Hebrew almuggim / algummim, most probably red sandalwood.
It is close-grained and fragrant, fit for building and for instruments of music.
Solomon made of it pillars for the house of the LORD and for the king’s house (1Ki 10:12).
Of the same wood were made harps and psalteries for the singers.
scriptures: And the navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones.
And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD, and for the king's house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day.
And the servants also of Huram, and the servants of Solomon, which brought gold from Ophir, brought algum trees and precious stones.
And the king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the LORD, and to the king's palace, and harps and psalteries for singers: and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah.
corruption_summary: The rarest timber went to God’s house first — a rebuke both to worship on the cheap and to worship as spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite corruptions meet at the almug. The first is worship on the leftovers: the congregation that gives God its scraps of time, its least prepared men, its unconsidered singing, its afterthought offering, while its own houses are panelled. Haggai named that sin plainly — “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4) — and Malachi named it sharper still, when the blind and the lame beast was brought to the altar and the governor would not have accepted it (Mal 1:8). Solomon’s ships fetched the best wood on earth and unloaded it at the temple before the palace. That order is the standing rebuke.

The second corruption runs the other way: worship as spectacle, where the “best” is defined by the eye and the ear of the consumer, and the house of God becomes a stage judged by production. The regulative principle answers both. God Himself appoints what He will have in His worship, and Solomon built by a pattern given, not by taste invented (1Ch 28:11–12, 19). Under the New Testament the appointed elements are plain — the reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, the singing of psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, the two ordinances, and the offering — and the “almug” the Lord now asks is the best of those: careful preaching, hearty congregational singing, reverent administration. The temple’s costly pillars have given place to a costlier building, for believers are now “an holy temple in the Lord” (Eph 2:21), and the finest timber He asks for is a living one.
roots_summary: The word names a rare imported timber reserved for the house of the LORD and for praise.
roots_lines: Almug — Hebrew almuggim; algummim in Chronicles.
Most probably the red sandalwood of the East, fragrant and close-grained.
It came from Ophir in Hiram’s navy with gold and precious stones (1Ki 10:11).
Solomon made of it pillars for the house of the LORD before the king’s house.
Of the same wood were made harps and psalteries for the singers (1Ki 10:12).
usage: Almug came from Ophir with the gold — and went to the sanctuary before the palace.
The rarest wood in the world was cut into harps: praise gets the best timber.
There came no such almug trees again; the temple had the finest of the earth once.

etymology: From the Greek thyinos, of the tree thyon — the sandarac or citron tree of North Africa, whose fragrant, richly-figured wood the Romans prized above all others for costly table-tops, single boards fetching the price of an estate.
biblical_def: Thyine wood appears once, and it appears in a cargo manifest under sentence of death. John lists the merchandise of Babylon the great: “The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood” (Rev 18:12). The Romans knew this timber well; a single burl table of citron-wood was the boast of a great house. It is not named as sin. Timber is God’s creature, and beauty is His invention. It is named because it stood in the inventory of a civilization that had made buying and selling its religion, and because that inventory has just become worthless: “the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more” (Rev 18:11). Mark where the catalogue ends — with “slaves, and souls of men” (Rev 18:13). A trade that begins with fragrant tables ends with trafficked persons; appetite ordered to no higher end will finally price anything. So the dirge is spoken over the whole desire: “the fruits that thy soul lusted after are departed from thee, and all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee, and thou shalt find them no more at all” (Rev 18:14). In one hour so great riches came to nought (Rev 18:17).
webster_summary: A fragrant, richly-figured African wood, prized by the Romans for costly furniture; listed among Babylon’s merchandise.
webster_full: THYINE WOOD, an aromatic and beautifully veined timber of North Africa, esteemed of great price among the Romans.
From the Greek thyinos, of the tree thyon, the sandarac or citron tree.
Its burls were sawn into single-board tables that cost the price of an estate.
It is named once in Scripture, in the merchandise of Babylon (Rev 18:12).
That merchandise no man buyeth any more (Rev 18:11).
scriptures: The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble,
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
And the fruits that thy soul lusted after are departed from thee, and all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee, and thou shalt find them no more at all.
Jas 5:2
Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten.
corruption_summary: A luxury timber under judgment — and consumption is the liturgy our own age has learned by heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is consumerism as worship, and Revelation 18 is its indictment. A liturgy has three marks: it tells you what is ultimate, it orders your time and treasure toward it, and it promises you a self. Modern consumption does all three. The advertisement is a sermon, the release date is a holy day, the unboxing is a testimony, the brand is a confession of identity, and the credit line is the vow that binds. Christ named the rival god by his proper name — “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24) — and warned, “a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). Babylon’s merchants weep not for her souls but for their sales. That is the tell: when the judgment falls, what the world mourns is its market. And the church is not exempt, for a congregation can carry the same catalogue into the sanctuary and call it blessing.

The principle to recover is that created goods are gifts to be received with thanksgiving and held with an open hand. Scripture does not despise fragrant wood, fine linen, or scarlet; God made the cedar and clothed the lily, and He “giveth us richly all things to enjoy” (1Ti 6:17). The sin is not possession but idolatry — the soul that lusts after fruits, and rests in them, and would not part with them. So the remedy is not asceticism but a better treasure: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt… but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:19–20). James says the same in the past tense, as though the ruin were already accomplished: “Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten” (Jas 5:2). Every thyine table on earth is already dust in the sight of the LORD; the only goods that survive the hour of judgment are the ones sent on ahead.
roots_summary: The word names an aromatic African timber, the boast of Roman luxury, listed in Babylon’s doomed cargo.
roots_lines: Thyine wood — Greek thyinos, of the tree thyon.
It is the sandarac or citron tree of North Africa, fragrant and richly veined.
Roman luxury paid the price of an estate for a single board of it.
It stands once in Scripture, in the merchandise of Babylon (Rev 18:12).
That catalogue ends with “slaves, and souls of men” (Rev 18:13).
usage: Thyine wood was the finest table in Rome — and a line item in Babylon’s fall.
The merchants wept for their merchandise, not for the souls: that is the mark of the trade.
The fruits thy soul lusted after are departed — luxury cannot survive the hour of judgment.

etymology: From the Hebrew gopher, a word occurring once in Scripture and left untranslated by the AV. It denotes a resinous timber, most probably cypress, whose oily grain both resists water and takes pitch; the noun is close kin to kopher, the pitch itself, and to kaphar, “to cover, to make atonement.”
biblical_def: Gopher wood is the timber God named for the ark. “Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch” (Gen 6:14). Every particular was appointed: the material, the rooms, the pitch inside and out, the length and breadth and height, one window above, and “the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof” (Gen 6:16). Noah chose nothing. He was given a word, and “thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he” (Gen 6:22) — a hundred and twenty years of obedience to a warning of things not seen as yet (Heb 11:7). Herein is the doctrine of salvation by God’s appointed means alone. There was one ark and no second; one door and no window at the waterline; and when the hour came, “the LORD shut him in” (Gen 7:16). Outside that door every other refuge was as sound as reason could wish and every one of them drowned. The pitch preaches the same gospel in Hebrew: the ark was covered with kopher, from the root kaphar, the very word of the mercy seat and the day of atonement — covered within and without, so that the judgment which bore up the ark never touched those inside it. Peter reads the ark as the figure of our salvation, “wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water” (1Pe 3:20). And Christ says plainly what the door in the side means: “I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved” (Joh 10:9).
webster_summary: The timber God appointed for Noah’s ark; a resinous wood, most probably cypress, pitched within and without.
webster_full: GOPHER WOOD, the wood of which the ark of Noah was built, by divine appointment.
From the Hebrew gopher, a word occurring only in Gen 6:14 and left untranslated.
It is most probably cypress — resinous, water-resisting, and apt to take pitch.
It is kin to kopher, pitch, and kaphar, “to cover, to make atonement.”
Noah did not choose the timber; God named it, with the rooms, the door, and the measure.
scriptures: Gen 6:14
Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch.
Gen 6:16
A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.
Heb 11:7

By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.
Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.
corruption_summary: One ark, one door, one appointed timber — the plainest rebuke in Scripture to the doctrine that many roads lead home.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is religious pluralism, the settled creed of the West: that the roads are many and the mountain one, that sincerity saves, and that to insist on a single door is arrogance. Genesis 6 answers it with carpentry. God did not present Noah with options; He named the wood, the measure, the pitch, and the door, and outside that vessel the finest raft ever built went down. The apostles preached the same exclusivity without apology — “Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12) — and Christ Himself said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). The narrowness is not the church’s invention; it is the mercy’s shape. A door is narrow because it is a door, and a door is the kindest thing in a wall.

A second corruption attends the first: the reduction of the flood to legend. Once Genesis 6–9 is treated as borrowed folklore rather than history, the ark stops being a rescue and becomes a symbol, and a symbol saves nobody. Scripture will not permit it. Our Lord grounded His teaching on the last judgment in the historicity of the days of Noah and the actual entering of the actual ark (Mat 24:37–39); Peter grounds the certainty of the fire to come on the fact of the water that was (2Pe 3:5–7). Deny the flood and you have unmoored the warning. Believe it, and the gopher-wood ark preaches: judgment is real, it is announced beforehand in longsuffering, the means of escape is God’s to appoint and not ours to invent, and the door stands open until the LORD Himself shuts it.
roots_summary: The word names the one timber God appointed for the ark — pitched within and without, and pierced with a single door.
roots_lines: Gopher wood — Hebrew gopher, occurring once, in Gen 6:14.
It denotes a resinous, water-resisting timber, most probably cypress.
It is kin to kopher, pitch, and to kaphar, “to cover, to make atonement.”
The ark was pitched within and without — covered from the judgment it floated upon.
It had one door in the side, and the LORD shut Noah in (Gen 6:16; 7:16).
usage: Make thee an ark of gopher wood: Noah chose neither the timber nor the terms.
One ark, one door, one appointed wood — salvation is by God’s means or not at all.
The ark was pitched within and without, and the LORD shut him in: covered, and kept.

etymology: The AV spells it chesnut, from the Old French chastaigne and the Latin castanea. It renders the Hebrew 'armon, from a root meaning “to strip bare,” and denotes most probably the plane tree, whose bark peels away in pale patches from the trunk.
biblical_def: The chesnut of the AV is a great water-loving tree of the streams, and it stands in two passages that between them teach the whole doctrine of means. The first is Jacob at Padan-aram: “And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods” (Gen 30:37). He set the peeled rods in the watering troughs, “and the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted” (Gen 30:39). The narrative records what Jacob did without commending it; his device was the folk-craft of his day, and it had no power in it whatever. Scripture then supplies the true cause from Jacob’s own mouth: “Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” (Gen 31:9) — and he adds that the angel of God had shown him the ringstraked rams in a dream beforehand (Gen 31:11–12). The increase was providence, not technique. The second passage sets the tree in Eden: in Ezekiel’s parable of the Assyrian cedar, “the chesnut trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty” (Eze 31:8). Even so, that towering cedar was delivered into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen and cut down, “because thou hast lifted up thyself in height” (Eze 31:10–11). The chesnut thus marks both ends of the lesson: God gives the increase, and God fells the proud.
webster_summary: A great tree of the water-courses, the AV’s chesnut; most probably the plane, whose bark peels in pale patches.
webster_full: CHESNUT TREE, a large tree growing by the water-courses; in Scripture most probably the plane.
The AV spelling is chesnut, from the Latin castanea.
It renders the Hebrew 'armon, from a root meaning “to strip bare.”
Jacob peeled its rods and laid them in the watering troughs (Gen 30:37).
Ezekiel sets it among the trees of the garden of God (Eze 31:8).
scriptures: And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.
And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.
Gen 31:9
Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me.
Eze 31:8

The cedars in the garden of God could not hide him: the fir trees were not like his boughs, and the chesnut trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty.
corruption_summary: Peeled rods in a watering trough — the ancestor of every religious technique that promises to make God perform.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is technique-religion, and the Word of Faith movement is its boldest modern form. From Kenyon through Hagin, Copeland, and the “declare and decree” pulpits of our own decade, the teaching is that faith is a spiritual law and the believer’s spoken word the lever that moves it: say it, claim it, sow the seed, plant the offering, and the increase must follow. Strip the vocabulary away and it is Jacob’s peeled rods in the trough — a device supposed to compel a result. Genesis is careful to tell us it did nothing. The lambs came ringstraked because God gave them, and Jacob confessed as much (Gen 31:9). Every scheme that turns prayer into procedure ends in the same place: either the technique “works” and the man credits himself, or it fails and he is told his faith was too small. Both outcomes rob God of His glory and the sufferer of his comfort.

The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of means. God ordains the end and He ordains the means to it, and the means are real — Jacob did tend the flocks, Paul did preach, the farmer does sow. But the means are never causes in themselves; they are instruments in the hand of the God who “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Eph 1:11). Paul draws the line exactly: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6). So the Christian uses the appointed means diligently and rests the outcome wholly on God, which is the death of both superstition and sloth. That is why the ordinances are signs and seals and not machinery, and why prayer is asking a Father rather than working a law.
roots_summary: The word names a great tree of the streams — in Jacob’s hand a useless device, in Eden a lesser glory.
roots_lines: Chesnut tree — Hebrew 'armon, from a root meaning “to strip bare.”
It is most probably the plane tree, whose bark peels away in pale patches.
Jacob pilled white strakes in its rods and set them in the troughs (Gen 30:37).
The increase came not from the rods but from God (Gen 31:9).
Ezekiel ranks it among the trees of the garden of God (Eze 31:8).
usage: Jacob’s chesnut rods did nothing; God gave the increase and Jacob said so.
Peeled rods in a trough: the oldest form of the newest religious technique.
Not the chesnut trees of Eden could match the cedar — and the cedar was felled for pride.

etymology: From the Old Norse fyri, a fir. In the AV it renders the Hebrew berosh, the tall evergreen conifer of Lebanon — cypress or juniper — second only to the cedar for timber, and used for ship planking, temple floors, and instruments of music.
biblical_def: The fir tree is the AV’s emblem of the curse reversed. Isaiah sets it against the thorn: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” (Isa 55:13). The thorn is not a random weed; it is the signature of Eden’s ruin, sentenced upon the ground when Adam fell — “thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee” (Gen 3:18). To promise a fir where a thorn stood is to promise the undoing of Genesis 3, and to call it an everlasting sign is to say the undoing is permanent. This is no mere improvement of climate; it is the redemption of the creature itself, “delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God” (Rom 8:21). The same timber then serves the sanctuary: “The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). And it serves praise, for David and all Israel played before the LORD “on all manner of instruments made of fir wood” (2Sa 6:5). Hosea puts the last word into the mouth of the LORD Himself: to the Ephraim who has done with idols He says, “I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found” (Hos 14:8). The evergreen does not merely picture the blessing; God is the evergreen, and every grape a believer bears grows on His branches.
webster_summary: A tall evergreen conifer of Lebanon; the AV’s emblem of the thorn-curse reversed and of fruit found in God.
webster_full: FIR TREE, a tall evergreen of the cone-bearing kind, yielding excellent timber.
From the Old Norse fyri; in the AV the Hebrew berosh, cypress or juniper of Lebanon.
It was used for ship planks, temple floors, and instruments of music (2Sa 6:5).
Isaiah sets it in the place of the thorn as an everlasting sign (Isa 55:13).
The LORD likens Himself to a green fir tree from whom fruit is found (Hos 14:8).
scriptures: Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.
The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.
Hos 14:8
Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found.
And David and all the house of Israel played before the LORD on all manner of instruments made of fir wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals.
corruption_summary: A promise of thorns turned to firs — emptied by the popular piety that expects an everlasting disembodied elsewhere.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not a culture-war slogan but a settled error in the evangelical imagination: the Platonizing hope that treats the Christian’s end as a bodiless soul in an immaterial elsewhere, harps in the clouds, earth abandoned. On that scheme Isa 55:13 can only be a figure of speech, for there will be no ground for a fir to grow in. Scripture’s hope is otherwise and far larger. The curse fell on the ground (Gen 3:17), and what the curse touched the redemption reaches: the creature itself groans and travails and shall be delivered (Rom 8:20–22); the promise is “new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness” (2Pe 3:13); and the city comes down to the earth, where the tree of life bears twelve manner of fruits and “there shall be no more curse” (Rev 21:2; 22:2–3). Our Lord rose in a body that ate broiled fish, and the resurrection of that body is the pledge of the whole restoration.

The principle to recover is the completeness of Christ’s victory. He was crowned with the thorns of Genesis 3 before He undid them (Mat 27:29), bearing the curse in His own person — “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). The fir standing where the thorn stood is therefore not sentiment but the visible arithmetic of the cross, and it is called “an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” because nothing in the new creation can be reversed. Meanwhile Hosea guards the doctrine of fruit: the evergreen is the LORD, and from Him alone is our fruit found. The believer does not manufacture a harvest and present it; he abides in the tree and the tree bears through him (Joh 15:4–5). Sanctification, like the new earth, is His work finished in us.
roots_summary: The word names the evergreen of Lebanon — timber for the sanctuary, and the sign of the thorn undone.
roots_lines: Fir tree — Old Norse fyri; in the AV the Hebrew berosh.
It is the tall evergreen conifer of Lebanon, second only to the cedar.
It came for ship planks, temple work, and instruments of praise (2Sa 6:5).
It comes up instead of the thorn — the curse of Gen 3:18 reversed (Isa 55:13).
The LORD compares Himself to a green fir tree, the source of His people’s fruit (Hos 14:8).
usage: Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree: Genesis 3 running backward.
The glory of Lebanon comes to beautify the sanctuary — the fir among the first.
I am like a green fir tree: the fruit a believer bears grows on Another’s branches.

etymology: From the Latin buxus and the Greek pyxos, the box. In the AV it renders the Hebrew te'ashshur, a slow-growing evergreen of hard, close, pale timber, prized by the ancients for carving and inlay and named among the trees the LORD promises to plant in the desert.
biblical_def: The box tree appears twice in Scripture, both times in Isaiah, and both times as something God plants where it could never have grown. The first is the wilderness promise: “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19). Every verb is His — I will plant, I will set — and the reason is given in the next breath: “that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it” (Isa 41:20). A desert does not sprout box trees. A grove of hardwood standing in sand is not an achievement of the sand; it is a signature. This is monergism written in horticulture: the LORD does not water a seed the wilderness supplied, He plants what was never there. Isaiah says the same of the men themselves — they are “trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified” (Isa 61:3), given beauty for ashes and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. The second occurrence gathers the same timber into worship: “the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). What sovereign grace plants in the waste, sovereign grace at last builds into the house of God. The desert grove and the sanctuary are the same wood at two stages of one work.
webster_summary: A slow-growing evergreen of hard, close, pale wood; in Isaiah one of the trees the LORD plants in the desert.
webster_full: BOX TREE, an evergreen of slow growth, bearing a hard, close-grained, pale yellow wood.
From the Latin buxus, Greek pyxos; in the AV the Hebrew te'ashshur.
Its timber was prized by the ancients for carving, inlay, and fine turning.
It is named among the trees the LORD sets in the desert (Isa 41:19).
It comes with the glory of Lebanon to beautify the sanctuary (Isa 60:13).
scriptures: I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:
The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.
Isa 61:3

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
Rom 8:21
Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
corruption_summary: “I will plant… I will set” — and the age insists the desert must first decide to grow something.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is synergism, and its popular form is decisional regeneration: the doctrine, spread through Finney’s new measures and hardened by a century of altar calls and sinner’s prayers, that the sinner’s free decision is the cause which turns God’s offered grace into an actual salvation. On that scheme the box tree plants itself and asks the LORD for water. Isaiah will not have it. The verbs are His: I will plant, I will set — and the stated purpose is that men may know “that the hand of the LORD hath done this” (Isa 41:20). Scripture is uniform: the natural man “receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God… neither can he know them” (1Co 2:14); the dead are quickened, not coaxed (Eph 2:1–5); we are born “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13). A desert contributes nothing to a grove but the ground it is planted in.

The principle to recover is effectual calling, and with it the assurance it carries. If the box tree planted itself, it may uproot itself; if the LORD planted it, then “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6). This is why the same prophet who names the desert planting can promise that the identical timber will one day stand in the sanctuary (Isa 60:13): what grace begins in the waste place, grace finishes in the house of God. And note that monergism does not make the believer passive afterward — the tree, once planted, genuinely grows, genuinely bears, and is genuinely called a tree of righteousness (Isa 61:3). Free will is not abolished; it is liberated. The desert is not consulted, but the grove is real.
roots_summary: The word names a hard-wooded evergreen — in Isaiah, a tree the LORD alone plants in the sand.
roots_lines: Box tree — Latin buxus, Greek pyxos; the Hebrew te'ashshur.
It is a slow-growing evergreen with hard, close, pale timber.
The ancients used it for carving, inlay, and the finest turned work.
The LORD sets it in the desert with the fir and the pine (Isa 41:19).
It comes with the glory of Lebanon to beautify His sanctuary (Isa 60:13).
usage: I will set in the desert… the box tree: every verb in the promise is God’s.
A hardwood grove standing in sand is not the sand’s achievement but God’s signature.
The box planted in the wilderness ends up in the sanctuary — one work, two stages.

etymology: From the Old English brēmel, kin to brōm, the broom — a low, prickly, scrambling thorn-shrub of waste ground. In the AV it renders the Hebrew 'atad and the Greek batos: a bush that gives no timber, little fruit, and no shade worth the name.
biblical_def: The bramble is Scripture’s emblem of the unfit ruler. Its great text is Jotham’s parable, spoken from mount Gerizim after Abimelech had hired vain and light persons and slain his seventy brethren upon one stone (Jdg 9:5). The trees go forth to anoint a king. The olive will not leave its fatness, the fig its sweetness, the vine its wine — each has a use, and each knows it. “Then said all the trees unto the bramble, Come thou, and reign over us” (Jdg 9:14). Only the useless bush accepts, and its acceptance is a threat dressed as an invitation: “If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow: and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon” (Jdg 9:15). A bramble has no shadow to trust in; a bramble is exactly what fire runs through fastest. Both halves came true, for within three years fire came out from Abimelech and from Shechem and devoured them each of the other (Jdg 9:20, 56–57). Our Lord uses the same shrub for a different edge: “every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes” (Luk 6:44). Nature governs fruit; a bramble cannot be argued into bearing grapes. And where judgment has fallen, the bramble takes the ground: “thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof” (Isa 34:13).
webster_summary: A prickly scrambling shrub of waste ground, useless for timber or fruit; the emblem of the unfit ruler.
webster_full: BRAMBLE, a prickly shrub of the waste places, yielding neither timber nor good fruit.
From the Old English brēmel, kin to brōm, the broom.
In the AV it renders the Hebrew 'atad and the Greek batos.
Jotham made it the king of the trees in his parable (Jdg 9:14–15).
Christ named it as a bush from which no man gathers grapes (Luk 6:44).
scriptures: Jdg 9:14
Then said all the trees unto the bramble, Come thou, and reign over us.
Jdg 9:15
And the bramble said unto the trees, If in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow: and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon.
Luk 6:44
For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes.
And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, and a court for owls.
corruption_summary: The bush that campaigns for the crown — the pattern of every self-appointed leader whose shade is imaginary and whose fire is not.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is self-appointed leadership, in the state and in the church alike, and Jotham drew its portrait three thousand years before the age of the platform. The fruitful trees decline the crown because they have work; the barren bush seeks it because it has nothing else. So it goes still. The man with a genuine calling to a real labour is reluctant to be made much of; the man with no fruit is available at once, and he arrives with the bramble’s two promises — a shade he does not possess and a fire he certainly does. The church knows this figure well: the leader who gathers a personal following rather than a congregation, who binds men to himself instead of feeding them, who threatens and flatters by turns, and who at last consumes the very people who anointed him. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that such men would rise “of your own selves… speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30).

The remedy is the qualification lists God has already given, and the plurality that guards them. Scripture does not ask who wants the office; it asks what a man is: blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, of good behaviour, apt to teach, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, not a novice, ruling his own house well and having a good report of them which are without (1Ti 3:2–7; Tit 1:5–9). Those are all fruit tests, and they are exactly the test Christ named — “every tree is known by his own fruit” (Luk 6:44). That word cuts twice. It disqualifies the bramble from ruling, and it disqualifies the barren professor from presuming, against the easy-believism that assures a man of heaven on the strength of a decision while his life bears grapes of Sodom. Elders are to be tried before they serve (1Ti 3:10), and every man is to examine himself (2Co 13:5); the bush that bears no grapes is a bramble, whatever it calls itself.
roots_summary: The word names a prickly, fruitless shrub of the waste — no timber, no grapes, no shade.
roots_lines: Bramble — Old English brēmel, kin to brōm, the broom.
It is a low, thorny, scrambling shrub of ruined and waste ground.
In the AV it renders the Hebrew 'atad and the Greek batos.
In Jotham’s parable it alone accepts the crown the fruitful trees refuse (Jdg 9:14).
It offers a shadow it has not, and a fire it has (Jdg 9:15).
usage: The olive, fig, and vine had work to do; only the bramble had time to be king.
Put your trust in my shadow — the promise of a bush that casts none.
Of a bramble bush gather they grapes? Nature settles fruit, and fruit settles the man.
